goals: Define a constitution and distinguish written from unwritten constitutions
Explain the five functions of a constitution

slides.heading: Constitution: Why and How?
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what a **constitution** is, what it does, and what gives it **authority**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: why rules, meaning, five functions, written and unwritten forms, and sources of authority
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Every group of people, from a cycling club to a country, needs rules. In this part we ask what a constitution is, what jobs it does for a society, and why some constitutions are respected while others are not. We shall use imagined clubs and countries to practise each idea.

slides.heading: What is a constitution?

rows: The body of basic rules and principles on which a country is governed
The written constitution of a republic
Basic rules collected in one authoritative document
Basic rules spread over statutes, conventions and decisions

visual.alt: Table of terms: a constitution is the body of basic rules and principles on which a country is governed; a written one is collected in a single document, as in India; an unwritten one is spread over statutes, conventions and decisions, as in Britain

slides.narration: A constitution is the body of basic rules and principles by which a country is governed. It can be written, collected in one document, as in India, which has among the longest written constitutions. Or it can be unwritten in the sense of having no single document, as in Britain, where the rules are found in statutes, conventions and decisions.

visual.alt: Web diagram: a constitution at the centre with five arrows to its five functions: basic rules for coordination and assurance, deciding who holds power and how government is formed, limits on the powers of government, aspirations and a just society, and the identity of a people
visual.caption: Five functions of a constitution.

slides.narration: A constitution does five jobs. It gives basic rules for coordination and assurance. It says who has the power to decide, and how the government is formed. It sets limits on the power of government. It lets a government fulfil the hopes of society and create conditions for a just society. And it expresses the identity of a people. We look at each in turn.

slides.heading: Function one: coordination and assurance

rows: Each family guesses when others will draw water
The timetable tells every family what to expect
A shared rule settles whose turn it is
No one is sure others will cooperate
Everyone can rely on the others

visual.alt: Two-column table for an imagined colony sharing a borewell: without written rules families guess and quarrel; with a timetable each family knows what to expect and can rely on the others
visual.caption: Function one: minimal coordination and assurance.

slides.narration: Imagine ten families sharing one borewell. Without a timetable, each family guesses, and quarrels follow. With a written timetable, everyone knows what to expect and can rely on the others to follow it. That is the first function of a constitution: a set of basic rules that allow minimal coordination and assurance among the members of a society.

slides.heading: Quick check: the meaning
slides.body_md: Which statement gives the standard meaning of the term constitution?
slides.narration: Choose the option that describes the basic framework on which a government is founded and run, not a single speech, order or list of laws.

slides.heading: Function two: who decides

nodes.label: It says how the government is formed

visual.alt: Flow: the question of who may take decisions is answered by the constitution naming the bodies and saying how the government is formed, so that power has a clear source
visual.caption: Function two: decision-making authority

slides.narration: A society must settle who may take decisions. A constitution names the bodies that make laws, carry them out and settle disputes, and it says how the government is formed. Without this, people would not know whose decisions count. This is the decision making authority function: it gives power a clear source and a clear shape.

slides.heading: Function three: limits on government

rows: Make laws through the proper body
Keep a person in prison without a hearing

visual.alt: Table for an imagined country: the government may make laws through the proper body, collect taxes and run schools, but may not imprison without a hearing, seize property without lawful permission or silence all criticism
visual.caption: Function three: limits on the powers of government.

slides.narration: Power can be misused, so a constitution also sets limits on what a government may do. Fundamental rights are a familiar example. A government may make laws through the proper body, but it may not keep a person in prison without a hearing. Because the limit is written in the constitution, even a government with a large majority must respect it.

slides.heading: Quick check: a limit on power
slides.body_md: A clause forbids the ruler to seize property without a court order. Is it a limit on the power of government?
slides.narration: Ask whether the clause holds back what the ruler may do.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: classify the clauses
slides.body_md: The imagined Charter of Norvale has five clauses. Name the function that each one serves.
bullets: Council of two houses makes laws: **decision-making authority**
No fine without a written reason: **limits on government**
A school in every district: **aspirations**
Opening lines on a shared past: **identity**

headers: Clause in the imagined Charter of Norvale
rows: Laws are made by a Council of two houses
No one may be fined without a written reason
The state shall run a school in every district
The opening lines recall the islanders' shared past
Every citizen files tax returns by one fixed date

visual.alt: Worked example table that links five clauses of an imagined charter to the functions of a constitution: law-making body to decision-making authority, written reasons to limits, schools to aspirations, opening lines to identity and a fixed tax date to coordination
visual.caption: An imagined charter, clause by clause.

slides.narration: Let us classify clauses from an imagined charter. A council of two houses that makes laws shows decision making authority. A rule that no one may be fined without a written reason limits the government. A school in every district shows aspirations. Opening lines on a shared past express identity. A fixed date for tax returns gives coordination and assurance.

slides.heading: Functions four and five

rows: Lets government act on a society's hopes and create conditions for a just society
Records the values a people share and wish to be known by

visual.alt: Table of functions four and five: enabling the government to meet the aspirations of society and create a just society, and expressing the fundamental identity of a people

slides.narration: The fourth function is to enable the government to fulfil the aspirations of a society and to create the conditions for a just society. A constitution gives a government the means and the direction to act. The fifth function is to express the fundamental identity of a people, by recording the values that they share and wish to be known by.

slides.heading: Quick check: identity
slides.body_md: The opening part of the imagined Charter of the Tamsa Isles recalls the islanders' shared history. Which function is it?
slides.narration: Think of the function that records who a people are and what they value.

slides.heading: Written and unwritten constitutions

rows: One document, among the longest of its kind
In the text and its amendments
By the procedure in the text
Largely through ordinary law and practice

visual.alt: Comparison table of a written constitution as in India and an unwritten one as in Britain on form, where the rules are found, and how they change

slides.narration: Compare the two forms. In a written constitution such as India, the basic rules are in one document, which also tells us how to change them. In Britain there is no single document. The basic rules come from statutes, conventions and judicial decisions, and much change happens through ordinary law and practice. Both countries have fundamental rules; only the form differs.

slides.heading: Authority 1: who made it

nodes.label: Authority from the way it was made

visual.alt: Flow: a body drafts the constitution; the questions are whether it is seen as legitimate and widely accepted; if yes the constitution gains authority from the way it was made
visual.caption: Source of authority 1: mode of promulgation

slides.narration: Why do people obey a constitution? The first reason lies in how it was made, which is called the mode of promulgation. If the body that made it is seen as legitimate, and if the constitution is widely accepted, it gains authority. A text imposed by a small group without discussion starts with a weak claim to respect.

slides.heading: Authority 2 and 3: content and design

rows: Balanced: special majority, checks and balances
Change is possible but not casual
Rules altered at the will of whoever holds power

visual.alt: Table of institutional designs: too rigid cannot adapt and may be abandoned; balanced with special majority and checks and balances allows change that is not casual; too flexible lets those in power alter the rules
visual.caption: Source of authority 3: balanced institutional design.

slides.narration: The second source is the content. Fair provisions give everyone a reason to accept the constitution. The third is institutional design. A good design divides power and builds in checks and balances. It is neither too rigid, which means it cannot adapt, nor too flexible, which means whoever holds power can rewrite it at will. A special majority for change is a balanced answer.

slides.heading: Quick check: complete the idea
slides.body_md: A constitution allows minimal ___ and assurance among members of society.
slides.narration: Remember the first function: the missing word means working together.

slides.heading: Three sources of authority

rows: Who made it; is it widely accepted?
Fair; a reason for everyone to accept it

visual.alt: Table of the three sources of a constitution's authority with the test for each: mode of promulgation, substantive provisions and institutional design

slides.narration: Put the three sources together. First, the mode of promulgation: who made it, and is it widely accepted. Second, the substantive provisions: are they fair, and do they give everyone a reason to accept the constitution. Third, the institutional design: is it balanced, with checks and balances. Strong constitutions usually score well on all three.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a five-mark answer
slides.body_md: Question: *Explain the functions of a constitution using the example of a student council.* Plan five points.
bullets: One function per point
Apply each to the council
Bold the key word
About 100 words

rows: Coordination and assurance, with a school example

visual.alt: Plan for a five-mark answer on the functions of a constitution: one point for each of the five functions with an example
visual.caption: About 100 words: one function per point, each with an example.

slides.narration: For a five mark answer, plan five points, one for each function. Apply each to the student council. Rules for meetings give coordination. The way officers are chosen gives decision making authority. A ban on expelling a member without a hearing sets limits. A promise of fair opportunities is an aspiration. Its opening statement gives identity. Aim for about one hundred words.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Basic rules and principles by which a country is governed
Coordination; who decides; limits; aspirations; identity
Mode of promulgation; fair provisions; balanced design

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: the meaning of a constitution, its five functions, its sources of authority and its written and unwritten forms

slides.narration: To sum up. A constitution is the body of basic rules and principles by which a country is governed. It has five functions: coordination and assurance, deciding who holds power, limiting government, meeting aspirations and expressing identity. Its authority rests on how it was made, how fair it is, and how balanced its design is. It may be written, as in India, or unwritten, as in Britain.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Define a constitution in one precise sentence
Name all five functions; add an example to each
Use the three sources of authority as headings
Never say Britain has no rules; say it has no single document

rows: A constitution is only a list of rights
Rights are one of five functions
Britain has no single document, but it has fundamental rules
It comes from acceptance, fair content and balanced design

visual.alt: Table of common mistakes in Part 1 and what to write instead

slides.narration: A few tips. Begin with a one sentence definition. When a question asks for functions, name all five and give an example for each. For authority, use the three sources as headings. And take care with Britain: it has fundamental rules but no single written document. Avoid saying that a constitution is only a list of rights.

visual.caption: From the Nehru Report to the Constitution in force; equally spaced, not to scale.

slides.narration: Here are the main steps, equally spaced for clarity. In 1928 the Nehru Report outlined a constitution. In 1946 the Cabinet Mission plan provided the basis for the Assembly, which met in December. The Objectives Resolution was adopted in January 1947. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950.

slides.heading: The demand for a constitution

rows: An early outline of a constitution for India
Basis on which the Assembly was formed

visual.alt: Table of steps toward the Assembly: the demand grew within the national movement, the Nehru Report of 1928 was an early outline of a constitution, and the Cabinet Mission plan of 1946 was the basis on which the Assembly was formed

slides.narration: The demand for a constituent assembly grew within the national movement. Indians wanted to frame their own constitution rather than have one given to them. The Nehru Report of 1928 was an early outline of such a constitution. It did not become law, but it showed that Indian leaders could agree on a framework. In 1946 the Cabinet Mission plan opened the way for an Assembly.

slides.heading: How the Assembly was formed

rows: On the lines of the Cabinet Mission plan, 1946
Elected indirectly by the provincial legislative assemblies; princely-state representatives included

visual.alt: Table on the composition of the Constituent Assembly: formed on the lines of the Cabinet Mission plan; members elected indirectly by provincial assemblies with princely-state representatives; first meeting 9 December 1946; strength about 299 after Partition

slides.narration: The Constituent Assembly was formed on the lines of the Cabinet Mission plan of 1946. Its members were elected indirectly, by the members of the provincial legislative assemblies, and representatives of the princely states were also included. It first met on 9 December 1946. After Partition, its strength fell to about 299 members, as commonly taught.

slides.heading: Quick check: why committees?
slides.body_md: Why did the Assembly work through committees?
slides.narration: Think about how a large body can study many subjects in detail.

slides.heading: Who led the work

visual.alt: Table of roles: Dr Rajendra Prasad President of the Assembly, Dr B. R. Ambedkar chair of the Drafting Committee, Jawaharlal Nehru mover of the Objectives Resolution on 13 December 1946

slides.narration: Doctor Rajendra Prasad was the President of the Assembly. The Drafting Committee, which prepared the draft text, was chaired by Doctor Bhimrao Ambedkar. Jawaharlal Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution on 13 December 1946. Many other members took part, and the credit for the Constitution belongs to the whole Assembly, not to any one person.

slides.heading: The Objectives Resolution

visual.alt: Flow: the Objectives Resolution was moved in 1946 and adopted in January 1947; its ideals guided the Assembly and shaped the Preamble
visual.caption: From resolution to Preamble

slides.narration: The Objectives Resolution was moved by Jawaharlal Nehru in December 1946 and adopted in January 1947. It set out the ideals the Assembly would follow in its work. These ideals went on to shape the Preamble. Treat it as a statement of purpose that came first, before the detailed provisions were taken up.

slides.heading: How the Assembly worked

nodes.label: Proposals come to the full Assembly

visual.alt: Flow: committees study subjects, proposals go to the full Assembly, open discussion hears many views, and the Assembly aims at consensus
visual.caption: How the Assembly worked

slides.narration: The Assembly deliberated through committees. Each studied a subject in detail and brought proposals to the full house. Debate was open, and the Assembly aimed at consensus. Members came from many regions, communities and opinions, and the Assembly respected diverse views. It also built on the inheritance of the national movement, which had already discussed many of these questions.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false
slides.body_md: The framers of the Constitution copied each borrowed idea word for word.
slides.narration: Ask whether ideas from elsewhere were simply copied, or fitted to Indian conditions.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: evaluating a claim
slides.body_md: Claim: *The Constituent Assembly could not speak for all because its members were not chosen by all adults.* Evaluate it.
bullets: For: members elected indirectly
Against: many regions, communities and opinions
Against: committees, discussion and consensus
Judge with a reason

rows: State the claim in your own words
Give a point for it, with a fact
Give a point against it, with a fact

visual.alt: Worked example table with four steps for evaluating a claim about the Assembly: state the claim, a point for with a fact, a point against with a fact, and a judgement with a reason
visual.caption: Evaluating how representative the Assembly was.

slides.narration: Here is how to evaluate a claim. State it in your own words. Give a point for it with a fact: members were elected indirectly. Give a point against it with a fact: they came from many regions, communities and opinions, and worked through committees to reach consensus. Then judge, with one clear reason. Both views are respectable.

slides.heading: Was it representative? Two views

rows: Members were chosen indirectly, not by all adults
Members came from many regions, communities and opinions
Princely-state members came by a different route
Committees and open discussion heard varied views
So it may not fully speak for everyone
It built on the national movement and sought consensus

visual.alt: Two-column table of views on how representative the Assembly was: some argue that indirect election and the different route for princely states limited it; others argue that varied members, committees and consensus gave it breadth
visual.caption: Both views, so that students can judge with reasons.

slides.narration: Students of politics have discussed how representative the Assembly was. Some argue that indirect election, on a limited franchise, and a different route for the princely states, meant it may not fully speak for everyone. Others argue that its members came from many walks of life and that committees and open debate heard varied views. Weigh both and give reasons.

slides.heading: Where the ideas came from

sections.heading: 1. What is a constitution?
sections.body_md:
A **constitution** is the body of basic rules and principles by which a country is governed. It sets up the main organs of government, defines their powers and relates them to the people.

**Written and unwritten:** in a written constitution the fundamental rules are collected in one authoritative document. India has a written constitution, among the longest in the world. Britain has no single written document: its fundamental rules are found in statutes, conventions and judicial decisions.

key_terms.definition_md: The body of basic rules and principles by which a country is governed.
A constitution whose fundamental rules are collected in one authoritative document.
A constitution with no single document, whose rules are found in several sources such as statutes and conventions.

sections.heading: 2. Functions of a constitution
sections.body_md:
A constitution performs five functions.

1. **Coordination and assurance:** it provides basic rules that allow minimal coordination and assurance among members of society.
2. **Decision-making authority:** it specifies who has the power to make decisions and how the government is constituted.
3. **Limits on government:** it sets limits on the powers of government, for example through fundamental rights.
4. **Aspirations:** it enables the government to fulfil the aspirations of society and to create the conditions for a just society.
5. **Identity:** it expresses the fundamental identity of a people.

key_terms.definition_md: Confidence that others will follow the same rules, which makes cooperation possible.
Basic rights guaranteed by the constitution, which the government must respect.

sections.heading: 3. Authority of a constitution
sections.body_md:
Why people accept a constitution depends on three things.

- **Mode of promulgation:** who made it, and whether it is widely accepted.
- **Substantive provisions:** whether the content is fair and gives everyone a reason to accept it.
- **Institutional design:** a balanced design with checks and balances, neither too rigid nor too flexible.

sections.heading: 4. The demand and the Constituent Assembly
sections.body_md:
The demand for a **constituent assembly** grew within the national movement. The **Nehru Report (1928)** was an early outline of a constitution for India.

The Assembly was formed on the lines of the **Cabinet Mission plan (1946)**. Members were elected **indirectly** by the members of the provincial legislative assemblies, and representatives of the princely states were also included. It first met on **9 December 1946**. After Partition its strength fell to about **299** members (as commonly taught). **Dr Rajendra Prasad** was its President, and the **Drafting Committee** was chaired by **Dr B. R. Ambedkar**.

key_terms.definition_md: A body elected or chosen to frame the constitution of a country.
The committee of the Assembly that prepared the draft of the Constitution.
Election of members by an elected body rather than directly by all voters.

sections.heading: 5. How the Assembly worked
sections.body_md:
The **Objectives Resolution**, moved by Jawaharlal Nehru on 13 December 1946 and adopted in January 1947, set out the ideals that shaped the **Preamble**.

The Assembly **deliberated through committees**, aimed at **consensus** and open discussion, and **respected diverse views**. Its members came from many regions, communities and opinions, and it built on the inheritance of the national movement.

**Some argue** that indirect election limited how fully it could represent all citizens; **others argue** that its varied membership and open debate gave it breadth. Weigh both views with reasons.

sections.heading: 6. Sources, borrowing and adoption
sections.body_md:
The **Government of India Act 1935** provided the base for many administrative provisions. Ideas were **adapted**, not copied, from other constitutions:

- **Britain:** parliamentary government, rule of law, the office of the Speaker, single citizenship.
- **United States:** a bill of rights (fundamental rights), judicial review, an independent judiciary.
- **Ireland:** Directive Principles.
- **France:** liberty, equality and fraternity.
- **Canada:** a quasi-federal form with a strong centre and residuary powers with the centre.

The Constitution was **adopted on 26 November 1949** (now observed as Constitution Day) and **came into force on 26 January 1950** (Republic Day). The Assembly took about three years, commonly given as 2 years, 11 months and 18 days.

key_terms.definition_md: The power of courts to examine laws and actions of government and to declare them invalid if they conflict with the constitution.
The powers not listed for any level of government, which in India rest with the centre.
A federal form in which the centre is stronger than the units.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying a constitution is only a list of rights; rights are one function among five.
- Saying Britain has no rules; it has no single written document.
- Writing that members were elected directly by all adults; they were elected **indirectly**.
- Confusing the **President** of the Assembly (Dr Rajendra Prasad) with the **chair of the Drafting Committee** (Dr B. R. Ambedkar).
- Writing that ideas were copied; say **adapted**.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: one correct option, date or term.
- 2 marks: two points, about 30–50 words.
- 3 marks: three distinct points, about 50–80 words.
- 5 marks: five points, about 80–120 words; for *evaluate* or *examine*, end with a judgement.
- Case-based (4 marks): read the passage first; name the concept for each line; part (c) has an internal choice.

cards.back_md: The body of **basic rules and principles** by which a country is governed.
One whose fundamental rules are collected in **one authoritative document**, as in India.
It has **no single document**; its rules are in statutes, conventions and decisions.

cards.front_md: How would you describe India's constitution in length?
cards.back_md: Written, and **among the longest** written constitutions.
Basic rules that allow **minimal coordination and assurance** among people.
Specifies **who has the power to decide** and how the government is constituted.
Sets **limits on the powers of government**, for example through fundamental rights.
Lets government fulfil **aspirations** and create conditions for a **just society**.
Expresses the **fundamental identity** of a people.
Confidence that others will follow the same rules.
**Mode of promulgation**: who made it and whether it is widely accepted.
**Substantive provisions**: fair content that gives everyone a reason to accept it.
A **balanced institutional design** with checks and balances.
One too hard to change; it cannot adapt to new needs.
One too easy to change; it gives little protection from those in power.
Each organ of government restrains the others so none gains unchecked power.

cards.front_md: Who put forward an early outline of a constitution in **1928**?
cards.back_md: The **Nehru Report**, drawn up by Indian leaders.

cards.front_md: On whose plan was the Assembly formed?
cards.back_md: The **Cabinet Mission plan, 1946**.
**Indirectly**, by the provincial legislative assemblies; princely-state representatives also included.

cards.front_md: When did the Assembly first meet?
cards.back_md: **9 December 1946**.
About **299** members (as commonly taught).
**Dr Rajendra Prasad**.
**Dr B. R. Ambedkar**.
Moved by Nehru on **13 December 1946**, adopted **January 1947**; its ideals shaped the Preamble.
Through **committees**, aiming at **consensus** and open discussion, respecting diverse views.
The **Government of India Act 1935**.
Parliamentary government, rule of law, the Speaker, single citizenship.
Bill of rights, judicial review, independent judiciary.
Directive Principles; liberty, equality and fraternity; quasi-federal form with a strong centre.
No: they were **adapted** to Indian conditions.
Adopted **26 November 1949** (Constitution Day); in force **26 January 1950** (Republic Day).

questions.stem_md: Which statement gives the standard meaning of the term constitution?

options.text_md: A list of laws that the legislature passed in one particular year
The body of basic rules and principles on which a country's government is founded and run
A speech in which a head of state describes the plans of the government of the day
A set of orders issued by officials to settle one particular dispute

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The body of basic rules and principles on which a country's government is founded and run. A constitution is the country's fundamental set of rules and principles. A list of one year's laws, a speech and a set of orders for one dispute are all narrower and temporary, and none of them is the basic framework of government.

questions.stem_md: Ten families in the imagined housing colony of Sundrapur agree to share one borewell and write down the hours in which each family may draw water. What does the written timetable give each family most directly?

options.text_md: Protection against misuse of power by an elected government
An expression of the fundamental identity of the colony's people
A statement of who holds the power to make laws for the state
Assurance about what the others will do, which allows minimal coordination

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Assurance about what the others will do, which allows minimal coordination. A shared rule tells each family what the others will do, which is the first function of a constitution: minimal coordination and assurance. A borewell timetable does not restrain a government, express identity or allocate law-making power.

questions.stem_md: The imagined republic of Veloria has a constitution which states that laws are made by a two-house Parliament and that the government is formed from the party or group with a majority in the lower house. Which function of a constitution is mainly at work here?

options.text_md: Specifying who has the power to make decisions and how the government is constituted
Setting limits on the powers of the government
Expressing the fundamental identity of a people
Enabling the government to fulfil the aspirations of society

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Specifying who has the power to make decisions and how the government is constituted. Saying who makes laws and how a government is formed is the second function, the decision-making authority. Limits on power, identity and aspirations are the other functions and are not what this clause deals with.

questions.stem_md: The constitution of the imagined state of Kandar says that nobody may be kept in prison without being brought before a judge, even if the head of government orders it. This provision mainly performs which function?

options.text_md: Providing minimal coordination among members of society
Creating conditions for a just society by directing government action
Placing limits on the powers of government so that they are not used arbitrarily
Fixing which institution has the authority to make laws

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Placing limits on the powers of government so that they are not used arbitrarily. A rule that even the head of government must follow restrains official power, which is the third function of a constitution. It does not coordinate private behaviour, set an aim for government or allocate law-making authority.

questions.stem_md: Which of these clauses in an imagined constitution best shows that it enables a government to fulfil the aspirations of a society?

options.text_md: A clause that fixes the number of members in the lower house of the legislature
A clause that stops the government from seizing property without a court order
A clause committing the state to widen schooling and to remove barriers of birth so that conditions for a just society are created
A clause that names the day on which the country observes its founding

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A clause committing the state to widen schooling and to remove barriers of birth so that conditions for a just society are created. A commitment to widen opportunity and build a just society equips the government to act on a society's hopes, the fourth function. Fixing house size allocates authority, the property clause limits power, and a founding day touches identity.

questions.stem_md: Why do we say that a constitution expresses the fundamental identity of a people?

options.text_md: It records the basic values and commitments that a people share and wish to be known by
It lists the name of every citizen who lives in the country
It forces every person to follow the same language and customs at home
It forbids the people from ever changing their way of life

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It records the basic values and commitments that a people share and wish to be known by. A constitution states the principles a people have chosen for their common life, so it says who they are and what they stand for. It is not a register of citizens, it does not impose one culture and it does not freeze social life.

questions.stem_md: The opening part of the imagined Charter of the Tamsa Isles recalls the islanders' shared history of living by the sea, and declares the kind of fair and welcoming society they wish to build. Which function does this opening mainly serve?

options.text_md: Setting limits on the powers of government
Allowing minimal coordination and assurance among individuals
Specifying who has the power to take decisions
Expressing the fundamental identity of the people

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Expressing the fundamental identity of the people. Describing a people's shared past and the values they commit to is an expression of identity, the fifth function. The opening says nothing about restraining power, coordinating individuals or allocating decision-making authority.

questions.stem_md: Which statement correctly contrasts a country with a written constitution with one that has no single written constitutional document, as Britain is commonly described?

options.text_md: The first has no courts, while the second has courts that make all the laws
In the first the fundamental rules are collected in one authoritative document; in the second they are found in several sources such as statutes, conventions and judicial decisions
The second has no rules at all about how the country is governed
The first can never be amended, while the second can be changed only by a king or queen

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** In the first the fundamental rules are collected in one authoritative document; in the second they are found in several sources such as statutes, conventions and judicial decisions. Even without one document, Britain is governed by fundamental rules drawn from statutes, conventions and decisions. Both kinds of country have courts, an unwritten constitution is not an absence of rules, and written constitutions usually carry an amending procedure.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined republic of Marnia a constitution was drafted by a small circle of advisers to one ruler and was announced without any discussion. On the ground of the mode of promulgation, why would its authority be doubtful?

options.text_md: Because those who made it did not speak for the people and it was not widely accepted
Because it was written in a language that few citizens speak at home
Because it contains too many articles for citizens to read
Because it describes the powers of the courts in great detail

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Because those who made it did not speak for the people and it was not widely accepted. The first source of authority is who made the constitution and whether people accept it as theirs. A narrow circle imposing a text weakens that. The language, length and detail of a text are not what this test examines.

questions.stem_md: A constitution in the imagined state of Orvale gives all the privileges to one group and leaves the others with almost none. Which source of authority is it most likely to lack?

options.text_md: A catchy opening declaration that is easy to remember
Fair provisions that give every group a reason to accept it
A printed copy that is available in every village
A large number of articles covering every subject

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Fair provisions that give every group a reason to accept it. A constitution earns respect when its content is fair and gives everyone a reason to accept it. Memorable wording, wide availability and length do not cure a text that favours one group.

questions.stem_md: The charter of an imagined hill republic can be changed only if every citizen, without a single exception, votes in favour. Which problem is the republic most likely to face?

options.text_md: The charter is too flexible and can be changed by any passing majority
The charter will give the courts no role at all
The charter is too rigid and cannot adapt to new needs
The charter will have no power to limit the government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The charter is too rigid and cannot adapt to new needs. When change needs unanimity, one holdout can block any amendment, so the text cannot keep pace with society. That is rigidity, not flexibility. Nothing in the rule says anything about courts or limits on the government.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined Republic of Sunmark, the party that wins a majority in one ordinary session can rewrite any part of the constitution by a simple vote on the same day. What is the main danger of such a design?

options.text_md: The constitution is too rigid, so no change will ever be possible
The constitution loses all its written form
The constitution can no longer name who makes the laws
The constitution is too flexible, so the basic rules can be altered to suit whoever holds power

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The constitution is too flexible, so the basic rules can be altered to suit whoever holds power. If a simple majority can change basic rules at once, those rules offer little protection and the framework loses stability. This is the opposite of rigidity. Writing and allocation of law-making are unaffected by the amendment rule.

questions.stem_md: What is the purpose of checks and balances in the institutional design of a constitution?

options.text_md: To merge all powers in a single body so that decisions are taken faster
To keep the courts out of questions about the legislature
To ensure that every office is held by the same person for life
To make each organ of government act as a check on the others so that no one organ gains unchecked power

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** To make each organ of government act as a check on the others so that no one organ gains unchecked power. Checks and balances spread power across institutions that watch and restrain one another. Merging power, shutting out the courts and permanent office-holding would all remove the checks.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A clause in the imagined Charter of the Tamsa Isles which forbids the ruler to seize anyone's property without the permission of a court is an example of a limit on the power of government.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** It restrains official power by making a court's permission necessary, which is how a constitution sets limits on the government.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Since Britain has no single written constitutional document, it has no fundamental rules about how its government works.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Its fundamental rules exist, but are found in several sources such as statutes, conventions and judicial decisions rather than in one text.

questions.stem_md: A constitution provides a set of basic rules that allow minimal ___ and assurance among the members of a society.
questions.solution_md: The first function of a constitution is to allow minimal coordination and assurance, so that people know what to expect from one another.

questions.stem_md: Match each clause from an imagined constitution with the function of a constitution that it chiefly serves.

options.text_md: Every flat in the colony pays the same fee on the first day of each month
The council of ministers is drawn from the majority in the lower house
The ruler may not arrest a person without an order from a court
The state shall set up a school in every district

match_right.text_md: Deciding who holds the power to decide

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). A common fee rule coordinates private behaviour. Forming a government from the majority allocates authority. Needing a court order restrains the ruler. A duty to open schools directs government towards a just and educated society.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A constitution imposed by a small group is likely to find it hard to command the respect of the people.

**Reason (R):** The authority of a constitution depends partly on who made it and on whether it is widely accepted.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A: since authority rests partly on who framed the constitution and on wide acceptance, a text imposed by a few starts with a weak claim to respect.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A government that has won a very large majority in an election is still not free to ignore the constitution.

**Reason (R):** A constitution sets limits on the powers of government, so that even a popular government acts within those limits.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A: limits in the constitution bind every government, including one with a huge majority.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A constitution which can be amended only with extreme difficulty may fail to keep up with a changing society.

**Reason (R):** A constitution is meant to be a changeless text which should never be amended.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: excessive rigidity stops adaptation. R is false: a good design is neither too rigid nor too flexible, and constitutions usually provide a way to amend them.

questions.stem_md: The Nehru Report of 1928 is best described as

options.text_md: the first constitution of India to come into force
the plan under which the Constituent Assembly was formed
an early outline of a constitution for India drawn up by Indian leaders
the ideals resolution that the Assembly adopted in 1947

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** an early outline of a constitution for India drawn up by Indian leaders. The report was a proposal for India's constitution prepared by Indians, long before the Assembly met. The plan for forming the Assembly was the Cabinet Mission plan of 1946, and the 1947 ideals resolution was the Objectives Resolution.

questions.stem_md: On whose plan was the Constituent Assembly of India formed?

options.text_md: The Simon Commission report of 1930
The Cabinet Mission plan of 1946
The Objectives Resolution of 1947
The Nehru Report of 1928

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Cabinet Mission plan of 1946. The Assembly was formed on the lines of the Cabinet Mission plan of 1946. The Simon Commission and the Nehru Report came earlier and did not set up the Assembly, and the Objectives Resolution was adopted by the Assembly itself.

questions.stem_md: How were most members of the Constituent Assembly chosen?

options.text_md: They were elected indirectly by the members of the provincial legislative assemblies
They were elected directly by every adult in the country on one polling day
They were nominated by the Prime Minister of Britain
They were selected by lot from among the retired judges

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** They were elected indirectly by the members of the provincial legislative assemblies. Provincial legislators elected the members for the provinces, and representatives of the princely states were also included. There was no direct vote by all adults, no nomination from Britain and no lottery.

questions.stem_md: Who was the President of the Constituent Assembly?

options.text_md: Dr B. R. Ambedkar
Dr Rajendra Prasad
Jawaharlal Nehru
Mahatma Gandhi

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Dr Rajendra Prasad. Dr Rajendra Prasad presided over the Assembly. Dr Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee, and Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution; Gandhi was not a member of the Assembly.

questions.stem_md: A student council in the imagined Riverdale School wants to copy the Constituent Assembly. It gives one small group the task of turning the agreed principles into a written text for the whole council to debate. Which Assembly body did this group most resemble?

options.text_md: The provincial legislative assemblies
The Cabinet Mission
The Federal Court
The Drafting Committee

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Drafting Committee. The Drafting Committee, chaired by Dr Ambedkar, prepared the draft for the full Assembly. The provincial assemblies elected the members, the Cabinet Mission proposed the plan, and the Federal Court was a court, not a drafting group.

questions.stem_md: The Objectives Resolution moved by Jawaharlal Nehru in December 1946 is best described as

options.text_md: a statement of the ideals that guided the Assembly and shaped the Preamble
a detailed list of every Article of the final Constitution
an Act of the British Parliament giving India independence
the final vote by which the Constitution was adopted

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a statement of the ideals that guided the Assembly and shaped the Preamble. The resolution set out the guiding ideals and later shaped the Preamble. It was not a list of Articles, a British Act or the final adoption, which came in November 1949.

questions.stem_md: Why did the strength of the Constituent Assembly fall to about 299 members after the Partition?

options.text_md: The Assembly voted to remove members who spoke against the draft
Provincial legislatures recalled their members at the end of 1946
Representatives of the areas that became part of Pakistan no longer took part in it
The princely states were all excluded from it

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Representatives of the areas that became part of Pakistan no longer took part in it. After Partition the members for areas now in Pakistan left the Assembly, which reduced its strength to about 299 as commonly taught. There was no vote to expel critics, no mass recall and the princely states were not excluded.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined school parliament a draft rule is revised several times after open discussion until almost every class representative can accept it, instead of being pushed through by a narrow vote. Which feature of the Constituent Assembly's working does this resemble?

options.text_md: Its dependence on a single powerful ruler
Its election directly by all adults
Its aim at consensus after open discussion
Its decision to hold all meetings in secret

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Its aim at consensus after open discussion. The Assembly tried to reach agreement through open discussion, as the school parliament does. It did not depend on one ruler, was not directly elected by all adults, and its debates were not secret.

questions.stem_md: Why did the Constituent Assembly do much of its work through committees?

options.text_md: Committees could study a subject in detail and bring a proposal for debate in the full Assembly
Committees allowed the Assembly to avoid discussion in the full house
Committees were required by the Government of India Act 1935
Committees replaced the need for a Drafting Committee

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Committees could study a subject in detail and bring a proposal for debate in the full Assembly. Working in committees let members examine subjects such as union powers, minorities and rights closely, and then place proposals before the whole Assembly. They did not replace discussion or the Drafting Committee, and the 1935 Act did not require them.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about the sources of the Indian Constitution is correct?

options.text_md: All its provisions were copied unchanged from the Government of India Act 1935
Nothing in it was influenced by the experience of any other country
Every feature was copied word for word from the constitution of the United States
Many ideas from the Government of India Act 1935 and from other constitutions were adapted to Indian conditions

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Many ideas from the Government of India Act 1935 and from other constitutions were adapted to Indian conditions. The framers drew on the 1935 Act and on other constitutions but adapted what they took. They neither copied one source unchanged nor ignored outside experience.

questions.stem_md: The idea of Directive Principles in the Indian Constitution is traced to the experience of

options.text_md: Canada
Ireland
Britain
France

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Ireland. Directive Principles are commonly traced to the Irish constitution. Canada is linked with the strong centre, Britain with parliamentary government, and France with liberty, equality and fraternity.

questions.stem_md: A student notes that the Indian Constitution creates a federation with a strong centre in which the powers not listed anywhere remain with the centre. From which country's model was this idea mainly adapted?

options.text_md: Canada
The United States
Ireland
Britain

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Canada. A quasi-federal form, with a strong centre and residuary powers held by the centre, is drawn from Canada. The United States is linked with a bill of rights and judicial review, Ireland with Directive Principles and Britain with parliamentary government.

questions.stem_md: Which pairing of a feature with the country whose experience it is commonly traced to is correct?

options.text_md: Parliamentary government: France
Judicial review and a bill of rights: the United States
Directive Principles: Canada
Single citizenship: Ireland

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Judicial review and a bill of rights: the United States. Judicial review and a bill of rights are traced to the United States. Parliamentary government and single citizenship come from Britain, Directive Principles from Ireland, and the ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity from France.

questions.stem_md: Which earlier law provided the base for many administrative provisions of the Indian Constitution?

options.text_md: The Indian Independence Act 1947
The Regulating Act of 1773
The Government of India Act 1935
The Morley-Minto reforms of 1909

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The Government of India Act 1935. Many administrative arrangements were carried forward from the Government of India Act 1935. The other options are different laws and do not serve as the base of the Constitution's administrative provisions.

questions.stem_md: In the Riverdale School quiz, the question is: which pair of dates marks the adoption of the Indian Constitution and its coming into force?

options.text_md: 26 January 1950 and 26 November 1949
15 August 1947 and 26 January 1950
9 December 1946 and 26 November 1949
26 November 1949 and 26 January 1950

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 26 November 1949 and 26 January 1950. questions.stem_md: Define a constitution in one sentence, and say whether Britain's constitution is a single written document.
questions.solution_md: One mark for a correct definition and one for the point about Britain.

answer.model_answer_md: A **constitution** is the body of fundamental rules and principles by which a country is governed. **Britain** has no single written document; its constitution is found in several sources, such as statutes and conventions.

marking_scheme.step: Britain has no single written document

questions.stem_md: State any two functions of a constitution.
questions.solution_md: Any two of: coordination and assurance, decision-making authority, limits on government, fulfilling aspirations, expressing identity.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It provides basic rules that allow **minimal coordination and assurance** among people.
2. It **sets limits** on the power of government. (Any two of the five functions are accepted.)

questions.stem_md: In the imagined Greenfield Cycling Club, riders trust that others will follow the lane rules written in the club rulebook. Which function of a constitution does this resemble, and why?
questions.solution_md: Name the function and explain that shared rules let people predict one another.

answer.model_answer_md: It resembles the function of providing basic rules for **minimal coordination and assurance**. Because the rules are written and shared, each rider can predict what the others will do and plan accordingly.

questions.stem_md: Mention any two sources from which a constitution draws its authority.
questions.solution_md: Any two of: mode of promulgation, fair substantive provisions, balanced institutional design.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **mode of promulgation**: who made it and whether it is widely accepted.
2. Its **substantive provisions**: fair content that gives everyone a reason to accept it. (A balanced institutional design is also accepted.)

questions.stem_md: Why should the design of a constitution be neither too rigid nor too flexible? Give one reason for each.
questions.solution_md: One reason about rigidity and one about flexibility.

answer.model_answer_md: If it is **too rigid**, it cannot change with new needs and may be discarded. If it is **too flexible**, whoever holds power can rewrite it at will, so it gives no stable protection.

questions.stem_md: What was the Nehru Report of 1928? Why does it matter in the story of the Constituent Assembly?
questions.solution_md: Describe the report and link it to the growing demand for an Assembly.

answer.model_answer_md: It was an early outline of a constitution for India drawn up by Indian leaders. It matters because it shows that the **demand to frame our own constitution** grew within the national movement long before the Assembly met.

marking_scheme.step: Link to the growing demand for a constitution

questions.stem_md: How were the members of the Constituent Assembly chosen? Name the two kinds of members.
questions.solution_md: Indirect election by provincial assemblies, and representatives of princely states.

answer.model_answer_md: Members from the provinces were **elected indirectly**: the members of the provincial legislative assemblies voted for them, not all adults directly. **Representatives of the princely states** were also included in the Assembly.

marking_scheme.step: Indirect election by provincial legislative assemblies

questions.stem_md: What was the Objectives Resolution of the Constituent Assembly? Name the document that its ideals shaped.
questions.solution_md: A statement of guiding ideals, and the Preamble as the document it shaped.

answer.model_answer_md: It was a resolution moved by Jawaharlal Nehru in December 1946 and adopted in January 1947, setting out the **ideals** the Assembly would follow. These ideals shaped the **Preamble**.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Lakeside School council says it has copied a rule from a neighbouring school. What would it mean to say that, like the framers of our Constitution, the council has adapted rather than copied? Give one example from the Constitution.
questions.solution_md: Explain adaptation as modifying an idea for local needs, with a valid example.

answer.model_answer_md: It means taking an idea from elsewhere and **changing it to suit local conditions**. For example, the idea of a strong centre in a federation was drawn from Canada but fitted to India's own needs and history.

questions.stem_md: The imagined republic of Sundrapur has a charter which fixes who makes the laws, forbids arrest without a hearing and promises equal schooling for every child. Name the function of a constitution shown by each feature.
questions.solution_md: One function for each feature.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Fixing who makes the laws shows the function of **specifying decision-making authority** and how the government is constituted.
2. Forbidding arrest without a hearing shows the function of **setting limits** on government power.
3. Promising equal schooling shows **enabling the government to fulfil the aspirations** of society and create a just society.

questions.stem_md: Explain three conditions that help a constitution gain authority in the eyes of the people.
questions.solution_md: Mode of promulgation, fair provisions and balanced institutional design.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It should be made by a body that people regard as theirs and be **widely accepted**.
2. Its provisions should be **fair**, giving all groups a reason to respect it.
3. Its institutions should be **balanced**, with checks and balances, neither too rigid to adapt nor so flexible that it is altered at will.

questions.stem_md: Compare a written constitution such as India's with Britain's unwritten constitution on any three points.
questions.solution_md: Three valid points of comparison; each side stated.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Form:** India's rules are collected in one document; Britain's are spread over statutes, conventions and decisions.
2. **Finding the rules:** citizens can consult one authoritative text in India, but must look to several sources in Britain.
3. **Change:** in India amendment follows a procedure laid down in the text; in Britain much develops through ordinary statutes and practice.

questions.stem_md: Describe any three features of the way the Constituent Assembly worked.
questions.solution_md: Any three of: committees, consensus, open discussion, diverse membership, national movement inheritance.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It **deliberated through committees** that studied subjects in detail.
2. It aimed at **consensus** and encouraged open discussion.
3. It **respected diverse views**, since members came from many regions, communities and opinions, and it built on the inheritance of the national movement.

questions.stem_md: Name three ideas in the Indian Constitution that are commonly traced to the experience of other countries, and name the country for each.
questions.solution_md: Three correct feature and country pairs.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Parliamentary government** and the office of the Speaker: Britain.
2. **Judicial review** and a bill of rights: the United States.
3. **Directive Principles**: Ireland. (A strong centre from Canada and liberty, equality and fraternity from France are also accepted.)

questions.stem_md: Trace three steps, with dates, from the demand for a constitution to the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly.
questions.solution_md: Nehru Report 1928, Cabinet Mission plan 1946 and first meeting on 9 December 1946.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **1928:** the Nehru Report outlined a constitution for India, showing a growing demand.
2. **1946:** the Cabinet Mission plan provided the basis for forming the Assembly, whose members were elected indirectly by provincial legislators.
3. **9 December 1946:** the Assembly met for the first time.

marking_scheme.step: Cabinet Mission plan and election of members, 1946

questions.stem_md: The student council of the imagined Kiran Public School wants a written constitution. Using this council as the example, explain five functions that a constitution performs.
questions.solution_md: One function, each applied to the council.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Basic rules:** the council's rules on meetings and fees let members predict one another's behaviour, giving minimal coordination and assurance.
2. **Decision-making authority:** the constitution says who can take decisions and how the executive team is chosen.
3. **Limits on power:** it stops office-bearers from, for instance, expelling a member without a hearing.
4. **Aspirations:** it commits the council to creating fair opportunities for all students.
5. **Identity:** its opening statement tells everyone what the council stands for.

questions.stem_md: Explain what gives a constitution its authority. In your view, which source matters most, and why?
questions.solution_md: Three sources, the rigidity balance, and a reasoned judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Mode of promulgation:** the body that made it must be seen as legitimate and its work widely accepted.
2. **Substantive provisions:** the content must be fair, giving every group a reason to accept it.
3. **Balanced institutional design:** power must be divided with checks and balances.
4. **Flexibility:** the design must be neither too rigid nor too flexible, so that it can adapt yet stay stable.
5. **Judgement:** fair provisions may matter most because people obey what they find just, though acceptance of the maker also counts. (Any reasoned choice is accepted.)

marking_scheme.step: Neither too rigid nor too flexible
Reasoned judgement on the most important

questions.stem_md: The imagined republics of Hillmark and Plainmark have very different amendment rules. In Hillmark the constitution can be altered only by unanimous consent; in Plainmark any ordinary majority can alter it in a day. Examine the strengths and dangers of each design and say what a balanced design would do.
questions.solution_md: Strength and danger of each design and the balanced alternative.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Hillmark's strength:** the basic rules are very stable and secure.
2. **Hillmark's danger:** one objection can block any change, so the text may become outdated.
3. **Plainmark's strength:** the text can adapt quickly to new needs.
4. **Plainmark's danger:** those in power can rewrite the rules to suit themselves.
5. **Balance:** a sound design asks for a special majority and uses checks and balances, so change is possible but not casual.

questions.stem_md: Describe the composition and the working of the Constituent Assembly of India.
questions.solution_md: Formation, members, officers, method and ideals.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Formation:** it was formed on the lines of the Cabinet Mission plan of 1946.
2. **Members:** provincial legislators elected members indirectly, and princely-state representatives were included; after Partition the strength fell to about 299.
3. **Officers:** Dr Rajendra Prasad was President and Dr B. R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee.
4. **Method:** it worked through committees and aimed at consensus and open discussion.
5. **Ideals:** the Objectives Resolution guided it, and it respected diverse views.

marking_scheme.step: Formation under the Cabinet Mission plan

questions.stem_md: Explain how the framers of the Indian Constitution used the Government of India Act 1935 and the experience of other countries, and show that they adapted rather than copied.
questions.solution_md: The 1935 Act, borrowed features by country, and adaptation.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **Government of India Act 1935** supplied the base for many administrative provisions.
2. From **Britain** came parliamentary government, rule of law, the Speaker and single citizenship.
3. From the **United States** came a bill of rights, judicial review and an independent judiciary; from **Ireland**, Directive Principles.
4. From **France** came liberty, equality and fraternity, and from **Canada** a quasi-federal form with a strong centre.
5. These were **adapted** to India's needs, for example by combining federal features with a strong centre.

questions.stem_md: Some say the Constituent Assembly was not chosen by all adult citizens and so could not speak for the whole country. Others say its Constitution still enjoys wide acceptance. Evaluate the two views.
questions.solution_md: Points on each view and a reasoned judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Case for the doubt:** members were elected indirectly by provincial legislators, not by all adults.
2. **More on the doubt:** the representation of princely states was by a different route.
3. **Case for acceptance:** members came from many regions, communities and opinions.
4. **More on acceptance:** it worked through committees, sought consensus and built on the national movement.
5. **Judgement:** the Constitution's fair provisions and the Assembly's open debate gave it wide acceptance despite indirect election. (Any reasoned judgement is accepted.)

marking_scheme.step: Committees, consensus and the movement's inheritance

questions.stem_md: Read the passage, an imagined newspaper report, and answer the questions that follow. *(Written by SOYL for practice; the colony, newspaper and people are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Identify the lift clause.

**(b)** Decision-making authority and how the body is formed.

**(c) (i)** Link a common rule to confidence in others' conduct.

**OR (c) (ii)** Link secret drafting to the mode of promulgation.

questions.stem_md: Read the extract from an imagined school debate and answer the questions that follow. *(Written by SOYL for practice; the school, speakers and country are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Speaker 1 questions how the constitution was made.

**(b)** Speaker 2 points to fair provisions.

**(c) (i)** A reasoned view on acceptance and fair content.

**OR (c) (ii)** A step that improves acceptance with a reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The mode of promulgation: who made the constitution and whether it is widely accepted.

**(b)** Its substantive provisions, that is, fair content that gives everyone a reason to accept it.

**(c) (i)** **Yes, partly.** A constitution needs the people's acceptance to last, so fair content may not protect it when the maker lacks legitimacy. **No, partly:** over time, fair provisions can themselves win acceptance. (Any reasoned view is accepted.)

**OR (c) (ii)** It could hold a **public discussion and ratification** of the text by a body representing the people. This would help because the constitution would then be seen as **made with the consent** of those it governs.

questions.passage_md:
**Imagined debate in a school assembly: "Does fairness alone make a constitution legitimate?"**

*Speaker 1:* The constitution of Veloria was prepared by a commission appointed by one ruler, and the public was never asked about it. That alone should make us doubt it.

*Speaker 2:* But look at what it says. It treats every community alike, it limits the powers of the ruler and it is easy to amend through a special majority. Who made it matters less than whether it is just.

*Speaker 1:* A just text which people did not accept can still be cast aside when the ruler changes.

children.solution_md: A reasoned view on acceptance and fair content.

answer.model_answer_md: **Yes, partly.** A constitution needs the people's acceptance to last, so fair content may not protect it when the maker lacks legitimacy. **No, partly:** over time, fair provisions can themselves win acceptance. (Any reasoned view is accepted.)

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Suggest one step by which Veloria could win wider acceptance for its constitution, and say why it would help.
alternatives.solution_md: A step that improves acceptance with a reason.

answer.model_answer_md: It could hold a **public discussion and ratification** of the text by a body representing the people. This would help because the constitution would then be seen as **made with the consent** of those it governs.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage, an imagined panchayat meeting, and answer the questions that follow. *(Written by SOYL for practice; the village and people are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Unanimity makes change nearly impossible.

**(b)** One person's order can alter the rules at will.

**(c) (i)** A special majority sits between the two extremes.

**OR (c) (ii)** One harm of each extreme.

answer.model_answer_md: **Too flexible:** whoever holds power can rewrite the rules for their own benefit. **Too rigid:** the charter cannot adapt to new needs and may be ignored or abandoned.
